chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Term Sheet as a Document

lessons.title: SAFE, CCD and CCPS Term Sheets: How the Instrument Shapes the Document

children.text: In the six months since he signed ChaiCart's term sheet, Rohan has looked at two more deals. One arrived as a short note with an interest rate attached. The other was a two-page document he was told to "just sign, everyone gets the same terms." All three are startup investments. None of the three term sheets look alike, because each uses a different instrument, and the instrument decides what actually goes into the document.

body.text: The size of the cheque tells you almost nothing about the size of the term sheet. A ₹20 lakh CCPS deal can run to pages of negotiated clauses, while a ₹15 lakh iSAFE deal can be two pages with nothing to negotiate at all. Know the instrument, and you know what to expect on the page.

children.text: Three Deals, Three Instruments

Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares (CCPS), Compulsorily Convertible Debentures (CCDs) and SAFEs, in India almost always the iSAFE variant, are the three instruments an Indian angel is most likely to run into. All three end up as equity in the company. They get there by very different routes, and the term sheet for each looks the part.

children.text: CCPS: The Full Negotiation

ChaiCart's term sheet from the previous lesson is the heaviest of the three. A CCPS round fixes a valuation today, so there is a price per share to negotiate, a liquidation preference to agree, and usually board or observer rights and protective provisions on the table. That is exactly why Chapters 2 and 3 of this course exist: CCPS term sheets carry the most negotiable content, and getting each clause right matters most here.

body.text: If you only ever invest through CCPS rounds, everything in this course applies directly to your term sheets. If you also see CCDs or SAFEs, as most active Indian angels eventually do, you need this lesson before you need Chapters 2 and 3.

children.text: CCD: Debt Today, Equity Tomorrow
A
Compulsorily Convertible Debenture (CCD)

is debt that is legally required to convert into equity and is never repaid in cash. Companies raise bridge rounds this way when they need cash quickly but do not want to fix a valuation before the next real priced round. Until conversion, a CCD behaves like a loan: it sits on the balance sheet as a liability and usually carries a coupon.

markDefs.definition: A debenture (a form of debt) that must compulsorily convert into equity shares or CCPS, rather than being repaid in cash. Common for bridge rounds where a valuation has not yet been fixed.

children.text: Verve Fitness, a Bengaluru boutique gym chain, is six months from a Series A it expects to close at a much higher valuation, but needs ₹40 lakh now to open two more studios. It raises a bridge round of CCDs instead of rushing a priced round. Rohan puts in ₹10 lakh.

body.caption: Verve Fitness's CCD term sheet, key terms

cells: Next equity round of at least ₹75 lakh, or 18 months from issuance, whichever is earlier
None. The CCD is compulsorily convertible and is never repaid in cash.

body.text: That 0.01% coupon is not a typo. It is kept nominal on purpose, just enough to satisfy the legal definition of a debenture. Rohan's real return does not come from interest. It comes from converting at a 20% discount to whatever price Verve Fitness's Series A eventually sets.

body.title: Pricing the Conversion
body.prompt: Verve Fitness's Series A eventually prices its shares at ₹500 each. Rohan's CCD converts at a 20% discount to that price. What price per share does Rohan's CCD convert at, in ₹?
body.explanation: ₹500 × (1 − 20%) = ₹500 × 0.8 = ₹400. Rohan's principal, plus any accrued nominal interest, converts at ₹400 per share instead of the ₹500 a fresh Series A investor pays, so his ₹10 lakh buys more shares than it would have at the round price.

body.title: Why the instrument choice matters under FEMA

children.text: This gets technical, and it matters most when any investor in the round, Rohan included, is a non-resident Indian or a foreign entity.

Under India's foreign investment rules, only certain instruments count as equity and fall under the more flexible foreign direct investment regime: equity shares, and preference shares or debentures that are compulsorily and mandatorily convertible into equity within a prescribed period. A CCD that meets this test is treated the same as equity for FDI purposes.

content.text: Get the conversion mechanics wrong, for instance leaving conversion optional rather than compulsory, and the instrument can instead be treated as External Commercial Borrowing or ordinary debt: a completely different and stricter regulatory regime, with its own interest rate caps and end-use restrictions. Whenever a round includes a non-resident investor, have a professional check the instrument's FEMA classification before signing.

children.text: iSAFE: Skipping the Negotiation
The original
Simple Agreement for Future Equity (SAFE)

was created by the American accelerator Y Combinator to let a startup raise money fast without agreeing a valuation upfront. A SAFE is not itself a recognised security under the Companies Act, 2013, so Indian investors use iSAFE (India SAFE), an adaptation created by the Mumbai-based early-stage fund 100X.VC that converts into CCPS and is built to work within Indian company and foreign exchange law.

markDefs.definition: A contract giving an investor the right to receive equity in the future, typically on the next priced financing round, without fixing a valuation or issuing shares at signing.

children.text: PetalBox, a Bengaluru D2C plants-and-flowers subscription startup, is raising a ₹75 lakh pre-seed round entirely on iSAFEs. Every investor signs the same two-page document with the same terms. Rohan puts in ₹15 lakh.

body.caption: PetalBox's iSAFE term sheet, key terms

cells: Yes, to invest further in the next priced round
Next equity financing round, sale of the company, or dissolution

children.text: The
Most Favored Nation (MFN) clause

is the one term worth checking closely in any SAFE or iSAFE. It lets an earlier investor upgrade to the terms given to a later investor in the same instrument, if those later terms turn out to be better.

markDefs.definition: A clause letting an earlier SAFE, iSAFE or CCD investor elect to swap into the better terms given to a later investor in the same instrument.

body.title: A Later, Better Deal
body.scenario: Eight months after Rohan invests in PetalBox at a ₹6 crore cap, the company is short on runway and issues a fresh batch of iSAFEs to a new angel at a ₹4 crore cap, a noticeably better deal for whoever signs it now.
body.prompt: Rohan's iSAFE includes an MFN clause. What does that mean for him?
body.modelAnswer: An MFN clause lets Rohan elect to swap his terms for the better terms given to the later investor. Here, he can choose to have his ₹15 lakh treated as if it were capped at ₹4 crore instead of ₹6 crore, which converts into more shares once PetalBox eventually raises a priced round. Without an MFN clause, Rohan would be stuck with his original, worse cap, even though a later investor got a better deal for taking on less risk by waiting eight months.

children.text: When a Term Sheet Sets Both a Cap and a Discount

Neither Verve Fitness's CCD nor PetalBox's iSAFE combines a cap with a discount, but plenty of Indian term sheets do. When both are present, the investor is entitled to whichever produces the lower price per share, since a lower conversion price means more shares for the same money.

body.latex: \text{Conversion Price} = \min\left(\frac{\text{Valuation Cap}}{\text{Fully Diluted Shares}},\ \text{Next Round Price} \times (1 - \text{Discount \%})\right)
body.caption: The investor always converts at whichever price is lower, the cap or the discounted round price.

children.text: Choosing What to Ask For, as the Investor

An angel rarely picks the instrument. The founder or the round's lead investor usually does. What you can influence is what you push for within it. In a CCPS round, focus your energy on liquidation preference, pro-rata and information rights, covered in the next two chapters. In a CCD, negotiate the discount percentage and the mandatory conversion timeline, since a vague or distant conversion trigger can leave your money sitting as debt far longer than you expected. In an iSAFE, the template is rarely negotiable, so check instead whether an MFN clause and a pro-rata right are actually included, since some templates quietly leave them out.

body.title: Name the Instrument
body.question: A founder describes a deal: "It carries a small annual coupon, and it converts into equity either when we raise a proper priced round or after 18 months, whichever comes first, at a discount to whatever price we raise at." Which instrument is this?
body.explanation: The coupon and the fixed maturity backstop are the giveaways. CCPS and iSAFE do not carry interest, and plain equity shares are not convertible at all. A coupon, plus a conversion discount and a maturity date, is a CCD.

cards.definition: Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares. A priced-round instrument with a fixed valuation, the heaviest term sheet, and a full definitive document set: SSA, SHA and amended AoA.
Compulsorily Convertible Debenture. Debt until conversion, carries a coupon, and converts into equity at a discount to a future round's price or by a fixed maturity date.
Simple Agreement for Future Equity. In India, the 100X.VC-created iSAFE variant, which converts into CCPS. No valuation is fixed at signing, only a cap and/or discount for later.
The maximum company valuation at which a CCD or SAFE/iSAFE converts, protecting the early investor if the company's value rises sharply before conversion.
A percentage reduction applied to the next priced round's share price when a CCD or SAFE/iSAFE converts, rewarding the investor for coming in earlier and taking on more risk.
A clause letting an earlier SAFE/iSAFE or CCD investor upgrade to better terms given to a later investor in the same instrument.

points: The instrument, CCPS, CCD or SAFE/iSAFE, decides how heavy the term sheet is, not the size of the cheque.
CCPS rounds fix a valuation today and carry the most negotiable content: price, liquidation preference, board and information rights.
CCDs are debt until conversion, usually carry a nominal coupon, and convert at a discount to a future round's price or by a fixed maturity date, whichever comes first.
SAFEs, in India almost always iSAFEs, set a valuation cap and/or discount instead of a price today, and the signed instrument itself is often the only document needed.
When a term sheet sets both a cap and a discount, the investor converts at whichever price is lower.
An MFN clause lets an earlier investor upgrade to better terms given to a later investor in the same instrument, and is worth checking for in any CCD or SAFE/iSAFE.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal or investment advice. ChaiCart, Verve Fitness and PetalBox are fictional and used for illustration. Instrument terms such as coupon rates, discounts and valuation caps vary by deal and change with market practice, and any round involving a non-resident investor raises FEMA and RBI compliance questions that need professional advice. Startup investments are high risk, illiquid, and can result in the loss of your entire capital.
